suggestions.rationale: A large matched U.S. Veterans cohort found substantially higher esophageal-cancer incidence among patients with achalasia than matched controls; cancers arising in the achalasia group were predominantly squamous-cell carcinoma. This supports focused cancer-risk review but not an automatic individual relationship. The generic esophageal-cancer catalog target is broader than the observed histology pattern, so pathology, chronology, treatment history, and other cancer risk factors must be reviewed explicitly.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Documented achalasia with chronic esophageal stasis/inflammation risk context → later esophageal malignancy, with histology and chronology requiring individual confirmation.
developmentQuestions: When was achalasia objectively diagnosed, and what testing established it?
What treatment was performed and what residual stasis, dilation, inflammation, or recurrent symptoms remained afterward?
When was the esophageal malignancy diagnosed relative to achalasia?
What histology was reported, particularly squamous-cell carcinoma versus adenocarcinoma or another tumor type?
What other esophageal-cancer risk factors and competing explanations are documented?
issuesToResolve: The cohort association does not establish that achalasia caused an individual patient's cancer.
The generic catalog target spans histologies; the observed achalasia cohort was predominantly squamous-cell carcinoma and should not be generalized to all esophageal malignancies.

evidenceGaps: Objective achalasia diagnostic records and treatment chronology
Endoscopy, imaging, and pathology documenting the later esophageal malignancy and histology
Records describing persistent or recurrent esophageal stasis/inflammation after treatment when present
Specialist assessment addressing chronology and other esophageal-cancer risk factors

sourceReferences.citation: Low et al., Risk of Esophageal Cancer in Achalasia: A Matched Cohort Study Using the Nationwide Veterans Affairs Achalasia Cohort, Am J Gastroenterol. 2024;119(4):635-645. PMID 37975607
sourceReferences.note: Nationwide matched Veterans Affairs cohort reporting higher esophageal-cancer incidence in achalasia and predominantly squamous-cell histology among cancers in the achalasia group; supports focused risk research, not an automatic individual conclusion.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 37975607; abstract/results; 1,863 Veterans with achalasia matched 1:4 to 7,452 controls; 17 versus 15 incident esophageal cancers; adjusted hazard ratio 4.6 (95% CI 2.3-9.2)
